name: Mimesis
statement: Art as the imitation or representation of nature, life, and human action.
statementAccent: the imitation or representation of nature
meaning: Mimesis, the Greek word for imitation or representation, is a foundational concept in ancient Greek aesthetics and the theory of art: the idea that art, whether poetry, painting, drama, or music, is essentially an imitation or representation of nature, life, human action, or reality. The mimetic theory of art holds that art imitates the world, and it was the dominant conception of art in the West for roughly two thousand years. The two great ancient treatments are opposed in their verdicts. Plato, in the Republic, is critical of mimesis: since the world of appearances is already a copy of the eternal Forms, a painting or poem that imitates an appearance is an imitation of an imitation, standing at a third remove from the truth, as with the three beds, the Form of the bed, the carpenter's physical bed, and the painter's imitated bed; mimetic art appeals to the lower, irrational part of the soul and can corrupt, so poets are to be restricted from the ideal city. Aristotle, in the Poetics, rehabilitates mimesis: imitation is natural to human beings, who learn from it and take pleasure in it, and mimesis, especially in tragedy, can convey universal truths, which is why poetry is more philosophical than history, showing what could happen rather than merely what did. Mimesis was challenged only much later, by Romantic expression theories and by abstract, non-representational modern art.
mechanism: The mimetic theory explains what art is and does by treating it as a representation of something in the world, and the ancients drew opposite morals from this. Plato's critique works through his metaphysics of Forms. The truly real is the eternal Form, the perfect pattern; a physical object, such as a particular bed made by a carpenter, is already only a copy of the Form of a bed; and the painter who depicts that bed produces a copy of a copy, an imitation at a third remove from the truth. Because mimetic art thus traffics in mere appearances rather than realities, and because, in Plato's psychology, it stirs and feeds the lower, emotional, irrational part of the soul rather than the rational part, he judges it epistemically and morally suspect and famously proposes to exclude much mimetic poetry from the well-ordered city. Aristotle reverses the verdict by reconceiving what mimesis achieves. He observes that imitation is natural to humans, that we are the most imitative of creatures and learn our first lessons through imitation, and that we take a distinctive pleasure in recognizing imitations. More importantly, he holds that poetic mimesis represents not merely particular events but the universal, what a certain kind of person would probably or necessarily do, which is why he says poetry is more philosophical and more serious than history, which relates only particular facts. Tragic mimesis, the imitation of a serious and complete action, arouses pity and fear and, through them, accomplishes catharsis. So for Aristotle mimesis is cognitively and morally valuable rather than degraded.

examples.text: Plato's painter imitates the carpenter's bed, itself a copy of the Form, so art stands at a third remove from the truth.
Aristotle held that imitation is natural to humans, who learn from it and take pleasure in recognizing imitations.
For Aristotle poetry is more philosophical than history because it shows the universal, what could happen, not just the particular.

variants.name: Plato's critique
variants.text: Mimesis as an imitation of an imitation, at a third remove from truth, appealing to the lower soul, warranting restriction of poets.

variants.name: Aristotle's defense
variants.text: Mimesis as natural, pleasurable, and conveying universal truths, with tragic mimesis achieving catharsis.

whyItMatters: Mimesis is the origin of representational theories of art and one of the most consequential ideas in the history of aesthetics. As the conception that art imitates or represents the world, it dominated Western thinking about art for some two thousand years, from Plato and Aristotle through the Renaissance ideal of art as holding a mirror up to nature and the doctrine that a poem is like a picture. The opposed treatments of Plato and Aristotle set the terms for enduring debates about the value and danger of art: Plato's suspicion that mimetic art deals in mere appearances and inflames the passions, and Aristotle's defense of it as natural, pleasurable, and a source of universal understanding, are the ancestors of centuries of argument about whether and how art teaches, moves, and matters. Aristotle's Poetics, built on mimesis, remains the founding text of literary theory and the source of concepts such as catharsis. The mimetic theory's eventual challenge, by Romantic expression theories that made art the outpouring of the artist's inner life and by abstract modern art that imitates nothing, marks a decisive turn in the history of art and aesthetics. As the idea of art as imitation, mimesis is a cornerstone of the philosophy of art.

working.text: understand a work of art as a representation or imitation of nature, life, or human action.
with Plato, fault it as a copy of a copy remote from truth, or, with Aristotle, value it as conveying the universal.
recognize that abstract and non-representational art imitates nothing, straining the mimetic theory.

limits: The mimetic theory, dominant for millennia, was eventually undermined as a general account of art. Romantic aesthetics shifted the emphasis from imitation of the world to expression of the artist's inner emotion and imagination, and, decisively, modern abstract and non-representational art, which imitates or represents nothing, showed that art need not be mimetic at all, so imitation cannot be the essence of art. Even within the ancient debate, much is contested and easy to overstate: Plato's exact target, whether all poetry or only certain kinds, and the scope of his exclusion of poets are matters of interpretation, and the beds passage is variously counted as at second or third remove depending on how one counts. Aristotle's key notion of catharsis, tied to tragic mimesis, is famously obscure and never clearly explained, so its meaning is disputed. Some datings and attributions reward care: On the ancient side the primary texts are the Republic and the Poetics, the phrase about holding a mirror up to nature is Shakespeare's rather than Plato's or Aristotle's, and Erich Auerbach's major modern study Mimesis dates to 1946. So mimesis robustly names the imitation theory of art, understood as a foundational but no longer universal account, opposed by expression theories and by non-representational modern art.
misreadings: Mimesis is not mere mechanical copying; ancient theorists understood it as representation, and Aristotle held it can present the universal rather than the particular. Plato's critique is not a simple dismissal of all art, but a targeted worry about imitation's distance from truth and its effect on the soul, and its scope is debated. And mimesis is not the essence of all art, since abstract and non-representational art imitates nothing, so treating mimesis as slavish copying, as Plato's blanket rejection of art, or as defining all art, misreads the concept.
origin: The ancient Greek conception, central to Plato's Republic and Aristotle's Poetics, of art as the imitation or representation of nature, life, and human action, the dominant theory of art in the West for two thousand years.

sources.text: Plato's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Plato's account of mimesis in the Republic, the three beds and the imitator at a third remove from the truth, the appeal of mimetic art to the lower soul, and the restriction of mimetic poetry from the city.

Aristotle's Aesthetics, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Aristotle's account of mimesis in the Poetics as natural to humans and pleasurable, poetry as more philosophical than history in depicting the universal, and tragic mimesis arousing pity and fear and effecting catharsis.
